title: Fifteen ragas
hookLine: his shabads are spread across fifteen ragas, the last in Jaijavanti, found nowhere else in the Granth
last: IT IS PASSING — IT IS PASSING.

lines: A TUNE THAT TAKES YOU SOMEWHERE.
cards: Some songs take you somewhere else the moment they start. A tune from a wedding, a lullaby a grandmother hummed, the radio in a hospital waiting room. Before any word arrives, the melody has already changed your mood.
Musicians in India have long organized that power into ragas: frameworks of notes and movement, each with its own feeling, often its own season or hour. The Guru Granth Sahib is built on them.
And one raga in it belongs, as far as the book is concerned, to a single Guru.

teach.h: THE GRANTH IS ARRANGED BY RAGA.
teach.b: Most of the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga. Past the opening prayers, you move through thirty-one raga sections: Sri, Majh, Gauri, Asa, and on.
Inside each, the hymns are grouped by Guru, and each is meant to be sung in that raga's mood.

teach.h: FIFTEEN RAGAS FOR THE NINTH GURU.
teach.b: Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads, commonly counted at fifty-nine, are spread across fifteen of them: Gauri, Asa, Sorath, Dhanasri, Bilaval, Ramkali, Maru, Basant, Sarang, and others.
You've already met him in Gauri, with pride and the passing creation; in Sorath, with the steady one and the friends who leave; and in Dhanasri, with the scent in the flower. Then there's Jaijavanti.
It's the last raga section in the Granth's order, and it's tiny: four shabads. All four are his. No other Guru, and none of the saints whose hymns sit in the Granth, has a hymn in Jaijavanti.
The sources don't say why he chose it, or why it appears nowhere else. Some musicians describe Jaijavanti as mixing two moods, a little longing alongside something bright.
And those four shabads are the ones you've just heard, remember, remember, and it is passing, with two more like them. The compilers could have tucked his hymns into a nearby raga.

teach.h: A ROOM OF HIS OWN NEAR THE END.
teach.b: Instead, the Granth gives the ninth Guru a short room of his own, near the end of the book.
The quiet voice has a raga of his own.

how: Ragis in the gurdwara sing Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads in the ragas the Granth sets them in, so the melody carries the mood the hymn was written for.

games.q: you're arranging the Granth, and the ninth Guru's hymns use a raga no one else's do. what does the Granth do?
o: fold them into a nearby raga.
give Jaijavanti a short section of its own.
games.why: Jaijavanti stands as the Granth's last raga section, with only four shabads, all by Guru Tegh Bahadur: a raga of his own.

practice: Play a recording of kirtan in any raga, ideally one of Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads, and for the first minute listen only to the melody: heavy or light, longing or bright, slow or urgent.
Then let the words come back in and notice how the mood carries them; if you can't play anything, hum one slow note and listen to it fade.

wordCard.voice: Fifteen ragas. Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads are spread across fifteen ragas of the Granth, and in one of them, Jaijavanti, every hymn is his.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: raag, a raga, a musical framework with its own mood. The Granth is arranged by raag.

carryVoice: Your line: a raga of his own. In music and in people, the mood arrives before the words do. See you tomorrow.
